clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Variceal Haemorrhage evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Variceal Haemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: vomiting large amounts of dark and bright red blood and dizziness for 2 hours

Key HPI features: Presents via ambulance with 2-hour history of vomiting two large basinfuls of dark and bright red blood mixed with clots. Reports profound dizziness, lightheadedness, and black tarry stools since yesterday. Known to have hepatitis C cirrhosis with portal hypertension diagnosed 4 years ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 122, BP 88/54 (haemodynamic shock). Airway assessment critical. Bloods: urgent FBC, coagulation (INR), LFTs, U&Es, cross-match 4-6 units packed red blood cells. Emergency upper GI endoscopy (OGD).
Relevant background/PMH: compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis, oesophageal varices Grade II seen on gastroscopy 2 years ago, portal hypertension
Current medications: propranolol 40mg BD (reports missing doses recently), spironolactone 100mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Variceal Haemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Severe peptic ulcer bleed without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness and profuse sweating with large-volume haematemesis — signs of haemorrhagic shock.
management_principles: Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G)
Resuscitate with blood products (restrictive transfusion target Hb 70-80 g/L to avoid worsening portal pressure)
Immediate IV terlipressin (2mg bolus) or octreotide to reduce portal inflow
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 55M with known hepatitis C cirrhosis and oesophageal varices presents with massive haematemesis, melaena, and haemodynamic instability.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 122, BP 88/54 (haemodynamic shock). Airway assessment critical. Bloods: urgent FBC, coagulation (INR), LFTs, U&Es, cross-match 4-6 units packed red blood cells. Emergency upper GI endoscopy (OGD).
reference_soap.assessment: Acute variceal haemorrhage secondary to portal hypertension in cirrhotic patient. DDx: severe peptic ulcer bleed, portal hypertensive gastropathy, Mallory-Weiss tear.
reference_soap.plan: Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G). Resuscitate with blood products (restrictive transfusion target Hb 70-80 g/L to avoid worsening portal pressure). Immediate IV terlipressin (2mg bolus) or octreotide to reduce portal inflow. Prophylactic IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1g OD) to prevent SBP and re-bleeding. Urgent emergency endoscopy for variceal band ligation. Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) or TIPS on standby if uncontrolled.

learning_objectives: Execute emergency stabilization protocol for massive upper GI haemorrhage including airway safety and large-bore access
Apply specific pharmacological adjuncts for variceal bleeding immediately upon presentation (terlipressin/octreotide plus prophylactic antibiotics)
Explain the rationale behind restrictive transfusion strategy (target Hb 7-8 g/dL) in portal hypertensive bleeding
Communicate urgently and calmly during a life-threatening gastrointestinal crisis

teaching.one_liner: Cirrhosis raises the pressure in veins around the oesophagus until one bursts, causing sudden, massive vomiting of blood — a life-threatening emergency.
red_flags: Dizziness and profuse sweating with large-volume haematemesis — signs of haemorrhagic shock

must_ask.say: How much blood have you brought up, and was it dark or bright red?
You mentioned swollen veins in your food pipe before — has a doctor told you about liver disease or varices?
Have you also had black, tarry stools?
Have you been taking your propranolol regularly?
Do you feel dizzy, faint, or sweaty right now?
Have you had any alcohol recently?
